standard: GDD rework v2 · 80+ researched scenarios · scorecard-passed
note: Understanding & supporting autism, ADHD & learning differences; accommodating, advocating, de-stigmatising (UNESCO 5.6, 1.3, 5.5). New v2 build, a Parent Layer pillar and a warm callback to Same Same, Different (g04): difference is wonderful, grown up for parents. It reframes neurodivergence as difference, not deficiency, and is strengths-first and never deficit-shaming. Six modes: understand your child (the common neurodivergences, strengths-first, your child's own profile and pace; different, not less; brains naturally vary), accommodate (adjust the environment and expectations to the child rather than forcing them to mask; sensory, attention, transitions, routines; accommodations give fair access like glasses, they don't spoil), advocate (you are your child's key advocate; school accommodations and family understanding and services, with rights under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016, which recognises autism and learning disabilities and mandates reasonable accommodation; seek assessment without shame), drop the shame and blame (it's no one's fault, not caused by parenting, screens or vaccines; meltdowns are overwhelm not naughtiness; you don't grow out of it; stop hiding it), strengths and wellbeing (build on strengths and passions, meet meltdowns with calm co-regulation not punishment, take co-occurring anxiety seriously, and see the whole wonderful child not a label), support and you (parent wellbeing matters and it is demanding, lean on peer parents and professionals, and it is not a diagnostic tool, pointing to professionals and routing parent burnout to Looking After You g63). Strengths-based and never deficit-shaming, never blaming parent or child, accurate and expert-reviewed; not a diagnostic tool. Builds on Same Same, Different (g04); a Parent-Layer pillar alongside Break the Cycle (g65) and Raising Gender-Diverse Kids (g66). India: neurodiversity is heavily stigmatised and under-recognised, with delayed diagnoses often blamed on parenting and school accommodations a fight, so the node de-stigmatises, helps parents seek assessment and support without shame, and points to rights under the RPwD Act 2016.

evidenceBase: Neurodivergence is a difference in how a brain is wired, not a deficiency, and the affirming approach is strengths-first: autism, ADHD and learning differences like dyslexia are real, recognised ways of being and learning rather than naughtiness, laziness or bad behaviour, brains naturally vary, and a neurodiverse child commonly brings real strengths (deep focus, pattern recognition and honesty in autism; energy, creativity and quick thinking in ADHD; big-picture and spatial thinking in dyslexia), though every child's profile is their own. Understanding a child's actual wiring, and seeing their strengths rather than only their struggles, shapes how they come to see themselves, and a diagnosis is a key to support, not a tragedy or a verdict (neurodiversity-affirming care; 'different, not less' and strengths-based research)

Support means accommodating the child rather than forcing them to mask, and advocating for their rights: it works far better to adjust the environment and expectations to the child (calm low-stimulation spaces, noise-cancelling headphones, visual schedules and routines, chunked tasks and movement breaks, respecting sensory needs) than to punish stimming, demand eye contact or force overwhelming situations, and accommodations give fair access like glasses rather than spoiling a child. Parents are their child's key advocate at school, with family and with services, and in India the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 recognises autism and specific learning disabilities and mandates reasonable accommodation, so seeking a professional assessment and support is wise parenting, not 'making a problem' or a sign of failure (accommodation and self-advocacy research; RPwD Act 2016)

Shame and blame help no one, while affirmation, co-regulation and parent support help everyone: neurodivergence is not caused by parenting, screens or vaccines, it is no one's fault and is lifelong, so meltdowns are overwhelm and communication rather than manipulation to punish, children need calm co-regulation, and hiding a diagnosis only feeds stigma and isolation. Building on a child's strengths and passions and taking co-occurring anxiety seriously grow their wellbeing and self-worth, the child is a whole person far more than a label, and the parent's own wellbeing matters too because the work is demanding, so leaning on peer parents and professionals and routing parent burnout to Looking After You (g63) is part of the support; the node is strengths-based, never deficit-shaming or blaming, and is not a diagnostic tool, pointing always to professionals (Same Same, Different g04; co-regulation and parental-wellbeing research; WHO/UNICEF inclusive parenting)

scenarios.hook: "A neurodiverse child is broken or less than other children."
scenarios.relearn: A neurodiverse child isn't broken or less; their brain is wired differently, different, not less.

myth.un: A neurodiverse child is broken or less than other children.
myth.re: Neurodivergence is a different way a brain is wired, not a fault or a lesser version; different, not less.

scenarios.hook: "Autism, ADHD and dyslexia are just labels for naughty or lazy kids."
scenarios.relearn: Autism, ADHD and dyslexia are real ways of being and learning, not naughtiness or laziness.

myth.un: Autism, ADHD and dyslexia are just labels for naughty or lazy kids.
myth.re: They're real, recognised ways of being and learning, not naughtiness or laziness; understanding them changes everything.
myth.why: A profile isn't a character flaw.

scenarios.hook: Sam: understanding how your child is actually wired is the first, biggest act of love. Sit right?
scenarios.relearn: Understanding how your child is actually wired is the first, biggest act of love.
scenarios.affirm: Truly understanding how your child is wired, rather than judging them by a typical template, is a foundational act of love.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a strength a neurodiverse child may bring, or a 'deficit' the old view focuses on?
scenarios.relearn: Deep focus and pattern-spotting are real strengths; the 'won't sit still, can't focus' view sees only deficits.

scenarios.hook: Match each neurodivergence to a common strength (every child is individual).
scenarios.relearn: Autism, ADHD and dyslexia each commonly come with real strengths, though every child's profile is their own.

scenarios.hook: You keep comparing your child to 'typical' milestones and feeling worried.
scenarios.relearn: Meet your actual child's profile and pace, not a one-size template that misses them.

options.text: Understand and support your child's own profile and pace
options.consequence: You meet your actual child, not a template.

options.text: Keep measuring them against a standard mould
options.consequence: Understanding your child's own profile meets them where they are; measuring against a standard mould misses who they are.

scenarios.debrief: Support your child's own profile and pace rather than measuring them against a typical template.

scenarios.hook: "There's one normal way for a child's brain to work, and my child should fit it."
scenarios.relearn: There's no single 'normal' brain; neurodiversity is natural human variation, and your child's mind is valid.

myth.un: There's one normal way for a child's brain to work, and my child should fit it.
myth.re: Brains naturally vary; neurodiversity is part of human variation, and your child's way of thinking is valid.
myth.why: Variation is the norm, not the exception.

scenarios.hook: Sam: when you see your child's strengths, not just their struggles, you change how they see themselves. Resonate?
scenarios.relearn: When you see your child's strengths, not just struggles, you change how they see themselves.
scenarios.affirm: Seeing a neurodiverse child's strengths, not only their struggles, shapes how they come to see themselves.

scenarios.hook: Spot the understanding that serves a neurodiverse child.
scenarios.relearn: Serve a neurodiverse child by understanding their different experience, not labelling them 'difficult on purpose'.

scene.text: 'My child's brain works differently, and that's okay'
'My child is just being difficult on purpose'
'Let me learn how they experience the world'

scenarios.why: 'Works differently and that's okay' and 'let me learn how they experience it' serve the child; 'difficult on purpose' doesn't.

scenarios.hook: Your child has just been identified as neurodivergent and you feel overwhelmed.
scenarios.relearn: A diagnosis is a key to understanding and support, not a tragedy; your child is the same wonderful child.

options.text: Take it as information that helps you understand and support them
options.consequence: The label becomes a key, not a sentence.

options.text: Treat it as a tragedy or a verdict
options.consequence: Treating it as helpful information unlocks support; treating it as a tragedy projects fear onto a child who is the same child.

scenarios.debrief: Treat a neurodivergence as information that helps you support your child, not a tragedy or a verdict.

scenarios.hook: "My child must be forced to fit the standard environment and behave 'normally'."
scenarios.relearn: Adjust the environment and expectations to your child rather than forcing them to mask and fit a standard mould.

myth.un: My child must be forced to fit the standard environment and behave 'normally'.
myth.re: It works far better to adjust the environment and expectations to the child than to force the child to mask who they are.
myth.why: Flex the setting, not the child.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a supportive accommodation, or forcing the child to mask?
scenarios.relearn: Headphones and visual schedules support; punishing stimming or demanding eye contact force a child to mask painfully.

scenarios.hook: Match each need to a practical home accommodation.
scenarios.relearn: Sensory overload, transitions and attention each have a simple, practical accommodation that helps a child thrive.

scenarios.hook: "Accommodations spoil a child or are unfair to others."
scenarios.relearn: Accommodations don't spoil a child; like glasses, they give fair access to the same chances.

myth.un: Accommodations spoil a child or are unfair to others.
myth.re: Accommodations give a child fair access to the same chances, like glasses for sight; they level the ground, not tilt it.

scenarios.hook: Your child melts down in loud, crowded places every time.
scenarios.relearn: Adjust for sensory overload instead of forcing it; a meltdown is overwhelm, not misbehaviour to punish.

options.text: Adjust plans and bring sensory supports to prevent overload
options.consequence: You set your child up to cope, not fail.

options.text: Keep forcing the situation and punishing the meltdown
options.consequence: Adjusting and bringing supports prevents overload; forcing the situation and punishing the meltdown harms a child who is overwhelmed, not misbehaving.

scenarios.debrief: Prevent sensory overload by adjusting plans and bringing supports, rather than forcing the situation and punishing the result.

scenarios.hook: Sam: a child who is accommodated can show you their best; one who is forced to mask is just surviving. Sit right?
scenarios.relearn: An accommodated child can show you their best; a child forced to mask is just surviving.
scenarios.affirm: When a child's environment is accommodated they can flourish and show their strengths, rather than exhausting themselves masking.

scenarios.hook: Spot the accommodation that helps a child thrive.
scenarios.relearn: Help a neurodiverse child thrive by adjusting the environment and building on strengths, not forcing suppression.

scene.text: Adjusting the environment to their needs
Forcing them to suppress who they are
Building on their strengths and interests

scenarios.why: Adjusting the environment and building on strengths help a child thrive; forcing suppression just drains them.

scenarios.hook: Match each setting to an accommodation that helps.
scenarios.relearn: Mealtimes, bedtime and homework each go better with accommodations that fit the child's wiring.

scenarios.hook: "If I accommodate my child, they'll never learn to cope with the real world."
scenarios.relearn: Accommodation builds the security from which coping grows; forced distress teaches fear, not real-world skills.

myth.un: If I accommodate my child, they'll never learn to cope with the real world.
myth.re: Accommodation builds the security and skills from which real coping grows; forcing distress teaches fear, not coping.
myth.why: Support is the launchpad, not the crutch.

scenarios.hook: You're unsure which accommodations your child actually needs.
scenarios.relearn: Tailor accommodations by observing and asking your child, rather than applying a generic checklist.

options.text: Watch, ask your child, and try supports to see what helps
options.consequence: You find what works for your real child.

options.text: Apply a generic checklist and ignore their cues
options.consequence: Watching, asking and trying tailors support to your child; a generic checklist that ignores their cues often misses the mark.

scenarios.debrief: Find the right accommodations by watching, asking your child and trying supports, not a one-size checklist.

scenarios.hook: "It's not my place to push for support; I should just accept whatever school gives."
scenarios.relearn: You are your child's key advocate; pushing kindly but firmly for the support they need is part of parenting.

myth.un: It's not my place to push for support; I should just accept whatever school gives.
myth.re: You are your child's most important advocate; pushing kindly but firmly for the support they need is part of the job.
myth.why: No one will champion your child like you.

scenarios.hook: "My neurodiverse child has no real rights to support in India."
scenarios.relearn: Your child has rights: the RPwD Act 2016 recognises autism and learning disabilities and mandates reasonable accommodation.

myth.un: My neurodiverse child has no real rights to support in India.
myth.re: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 recognises autism and learning disabilities and mandates reasonable accommodation, including in schools.
myth.why: The law is on your child's side.

scenarios.hook: Sort: effective advocacy for your child, or giving up their support?
scenarios.relearn: Written requests and calm evidence are effective advocacy; accepting 'just naughty' or hiding the diagnosis give up support.

scenarios.hook: The school dismisses your child's needs as 'bad behaviour'.
scenarios.relearn: Reframe 'bad behaviour' at school by explaining your child's profile and requesting accommodations, not accepting blame.

options.text: Calmly explain the profile and request specific accommodations
options.consequence: You shift them from blame to support.

options.text: Accept the blame and ask nothing
options.consequence: Explaining the profile and requesting accommodations shifts the school to support; accepting blame leaves your child unhelped.

scenarios.debrief: When school calls needs 'bad behaviour', calmly explain the profile and request specific accommodations.

scenarios.hook: Match each arena to an advocacy move.
scenarios.relearn: At school, with family and with services, advocacy means requesting accommodations, sharing understanding, and seeking support.

pairs.right: Request accommodations under the RPwD Act

scenarios.hook: A relative insists your child just needs 'strict discipline'. You want to advocate calmly.
scenarios.relearn: Calmly explaining that support, not harsher punishment, is what helps protects your child from misguided 'discipline'.

yourLine.text: "His brain works differently, and what helps him is support and understanding, not harsher punishment."
"You're right, maybe I'm too soft on him."

scenarios.hook: Sam: every time you advocate, you teach your child that they're worth fighting for. Worth it?
scenarios.relearn: Every time you advocate, you teach your child that they're worth fighting for.
scenarios.affirm: Each act of advocacy teaches a neurodiverse child that they matter and are worth standing up for.

scenarios.hook: Spot the advocacy that gets a child real support.
scenarios.relearn: Real support comes from knowing rights, asking clearly and partnering with school, not staying silent.

scene.text: Knowing their rights and asking clearly
Staying silent to avoid being 'that parent'
Partnering with teachers on a plan

scenarios.why: Knowing rights, asking clearly and partnering with teachers get support; staying silent to avoid fuss leaves the child without it.

scenarios.hook: You suspect your child is neurodivergent but worry that seeking assessment is 'making a problem'.
scenarios.relearn: Pursue assessment rather than avoiding a 'label'; understanding unlocks the support your child needs.

options.text: Seek a professional assessment; understanding helps your child
options.consequence: You open the door to the right support.

options.text: Avoid it so as not to 'label' them
options.consequence: Seeking assessment opens the door to support and understanding; avoiding it to dodge a 'label' delays the help your child needs.

scenarios.debrief: Seek a professional assessment if you suspect neurodivergence; understanding opens the door to support, it isn't 'making a problem'.

scenarios.hook: "Asking for help with my child marks me as a failing parent."
scenarios.relearn: Asking for help and accommodations is what good parents of neurodiverse kids do; it's strength, not failure.

myth.un: Asking for help with my child marks me as a failing parent.
myth.re: Seeking support and accommodations is exactly what good, informed parents of neurodiverse kids do; it's strength, not failure.

scenarios.hook: "My child's neurodivergence is caused by my bad parenting."
scenarios.relearn: Neurodivergence isn't caused by your parenting or by screens or vaccines; it's simply how your child is wired.

myth.un: My child's neurodivergence is caused by my bad parenting.
myth.re: Neurodivergence isn't caused by parenting, screens, vaccines or anything you did; it's simply how your child is wired.
myth.why: It's no one's fault, least of all yours.

scenarios.hook: "A child who melts down or can't sit still is just badly behaved."
scenarios.relearn: Meltdowns and restlessness are usually overwhelm or different wiring, not bad behaviour to punish.

myth.un: A child who melts down or can't sit still is just badly behaved.
myth.re: Meltdowns and restlessness are often the brain overwhelmed or wired differently, not naughtiness to be punished.

scenarios.hook: "They'll just grow out of it if we ignore it."
scenarios.relearn: A child doesn't 'grow out of' neurodivergence; understanding and support help them thrive, ignoring it doesn't.

myth.un: They'll just grow out of it if we ignore it.
myth.re: Neurodivergence is lifelong; understanding and support help a child thrive, while ignoring it leaves them struggling alone.
myth.why: Support helps; waiting it out doesn't.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a fact that lifts shame, or a myth that piles it on?
scenarios.relearn: 'No one's fault' and 'can thrive with support' lift shame; 'you caused it' and 'hide it' pile shame on unfairly.

items.text: Your child can thrive with support

scenarios.hook: Sam: you didn't cause this, you can't 'cure' it, and you absolutely can help your child flourish. Land okay?
scenarios.relearn: You didn't cause it, you can't cure it, and you can help your child flourish.
scenarios.affirm: You didn't cause your child's neurodivergence and can't cure it, but you can absolutely help them flourish.

scenarios.hook: Relatives blame you, or your child, for the neurodivergence.
scenarios.relearn: Shield your child from blame by correcting it calmly; don't pass undeserved shame on to them.

options.text: Calmly correct the blame and protect your child from it
options.consequence: You shield your child from undeserved shame.

options.text: Absorb the blame and pass it to your child
options.consequence: Calmly correcting the blame shields your child; absorbing it and passing it on hands your child shame they don't deserve.

scenarios.debrief: Correct relatives' blame calmly and protect your child from it; it's no one's fault.

scenarios.hook: Spot what helps a family drop the shame.
scenarios.relearn: Families drop the shame by knowing it's no one's fault and talking openly, not by hiding the child.

scene.text: Knowing it's no one's fault
Hiding the child from relatives
Talking about it openly and kindly

scenarios.why: Knowing it's no one's fault and talking openly drop the shame; hiding the child keeps the shame alive.

scenarios.hook: Sam: shame helps no one; your energy is better spent understanding and championing your child. Agree?
scenarios.relearn: Shame helps no one; spend that energy understanding and championing your child instead.
scenarios.affirm: Shame and blame help no one; that energy is far better spent understanding and championing your child.

scenarios.hook: "I should hide my child's diagnosis so people don't judge us."
scenarios.relearn: Hiding a diagnosis reinforces stigma and isolation; sharing on your own terms lets in support and understanding.

myth.un: I should hide my child's diagnosis so people don't judge us.
myth.re: Hiding it reinforces stigma and isolates you both; openness, on your own terms, lets support and understanding in.
myth.why: Secrecy feeds the shame it fears.

scenarios.hook: You feel grief and guilt about your child's diagnosis.
scenarios.relearn: Feel what you feel, drop the guilt, and refocus on your child as they are; guilt and what-ifs help no one.

options.text: Allow the feelings, drop the guilt, and refocus on your child as they are
options.consequence: You move from grief to engaged support.

options.text: Stay stuck in guilt and what-ifs
options.consequence: Allowing feelings and dropping guilt frees you to support your child; staying stuck in guilt helps no one and drains you.

scenarios.debrief: Allow grief but drop the guilt, and refocus on supporting the wonderful child in front of you.

scenarios.hook: "I should focus only on fixing my neurodiverse child's weaknesses."
scenarios.relearn: Build on your child's strengths and passions, not only their weaknesses; that grows confidence and skills.

myth.un: I should focus only on fixing my neurodiverse child's weaknesses.
myth.re: Building on a child's strengths and passions does more for their confidence and growth than fixating on deficits.
myth.why: Strengths are the foundation to build on.

scenarios.hook: Sort: nurtures a neurodiverse child's wellbeing, or chips at their self-worth?
scenarios.relearn: Celebrating passions and praising strengths nurture wellbeing; constant comparison and 'a problem' framing chip at self-worth.

items.text: Making them feel like a problem

scenarios.hook: "A meltdown is my child trying to manipulate or defy me."
scenarios.relearn: A meltdown is overwhelm spilling over, not manipulation; your child needs calm co-regulation, not punishment.

myth.un: A meltdown is my child trying to manipulate or defy me.
myth.re: A meltdown is usually distress and overwhelm spilling over, not manipulation; your child needs co-regulation, not punishment.

scenarios.hook: Your child is melting down and you feel your own frustration rising.
scenarios.relearn: Co-regulate a meltdown with calm and safety; meeting overwhelm with anger only escalates it.

options.text: Stay calm, keep them safe, and co-regulate until the wave passes
options.consequence: You help your child through the storm.

options.text: Match their dysregulation with anger
options.consequence: Staying calm and co-regulating helps the wave pass; matching it with anger escalates and frightens an overwhelmed child.

scenarios.debrief: Meet a meltdown with calm co-regulation and safety, not anger; it's a storm to ride out together.

scenarios.hook: Match each strength to a way to nurture it.
scenarios.relearn: An intense interest, honesty and creative thinking each grow when a parent nurtures rather than discourages them.

scenarios.hook: Sam: a neurodiverse child who feels celebrated, not just corrected, grows up liking who they are. Worth it?
scenarios.relearn: A child who feels celebrated, not just corrected, grows up liking who they are.
scenarios.affirm: A neurodiverse child who feels celebrated, not constantly corrected, grows up with self-worth and confidence.

scenarios.hook: Spot what supports a neurodiverse child's wellbeing.

scene.text: Noticing and easing their anxiety
Dismissing their distress as drama
Celebrating who they are

scenarios.why: Easing anxiety and celebrating who they are support wellbeing; dismissing distress as drama harms it.

scenarios.hook: Your neurodiverse child often seems anxious or down.
scenarios.relearn: Don't dismiss persistent anxiety as 'just the diagnosis'; take a neurodiverse child's wellbeing seriously and seek support.

options.text: Take their wellbeing seriously and seek support if it persists
options.consequence: You catch a co-occurring need early.

options.text: Assume it's just part of the diagnosis and ignore it
options.consequence: Taking wellbeing seriously catches anxiety early; assuming distress is 'just the diagnosis' can miss a treatable need.

scenarios.debrief: Take a neurodiverse child's anxiety or low mood seriously and seek support if it persists; co-occurring needs are real.

scenarios.hook: Sam: your child is so much more than a diagnosis; seeing the whole, wonderful person is everything. Sit right?
scenarios.relearn: Your child is so much more than a diagnosis; seeing the whole, wonderful person is everything.
scenarios.affirm: A neurodiverse child is a whole, wonderful person, not a diagnosis; seeing all of them is what matters most.

scenarios.hook: "A devoted parent of a neurodiverse child should run on empty and never need support."

myth.re: Supporting a neurodiverse child can be exhausting; looking after yourself and getting support helps you keep showing up.

"Maybe you're right, I should make him tough it out."

scenarios.hook: Sort: respects how the child is wired, or forces them to mask?
scenarios.relearn: Letting them fidget and giving quiet breaks respect the wiring; forcing stillness and punishing self-soothing force masking.

scenarios.hook: Your child copes best with strict routine, but plans change suddenly today.
scenarios.relearn: Prepare a routine-reliant child for change with warning and a visual; don't spring it and expect instant adapting.

options.text: Prepare them with warning and a visual of the change
options.consequence: You ease a hard transition for them.

options.text: Spring the change and expect them to just adapt
options.consequence: Warning and a visual ease a hard transition; springing change on a child who needs routine sets them up to be overwhelmed.

scenarios.debrief: Ease sudden changes for a routine-reliant child with warning and a visual, rather than springing it on them.

scenarios.hook: Match each tricky moment to the accommodation that helps.
scenarios.relearn: Parties, new places and big feelings each go better with a simple accommodation than with force.

pairs.right: A quiet exit plan and headphones
Visit or preview it in advance
A calm-down space, not a telling-off

scenarios.hook: You're meeting your child's teacher to request support. You want to open as a partner, not a complainer.
scenarios.relearn: Opening as a collaborative partner, with what helps, gets a teacher on side far better than blame.

yourLine.text: "I'd love to work with you so he can do his best, here's what helps him, and what could we try together?"
"Your class is failing my child and it's your fault."

scenarios.hook: Sort: strengthens your advocacy, or weakens it?
scenarios.relearn: Documentation and knowing the law strengthen advocacy; giving up after one 'no' or over-apologising weaken it.

scenarios.hook: A service is slow and dismissive about assessing your child.
scenarios.relearn: Keep advocating through slow services; one dismissal isn't the end of the road to support.

options.text: Persist politely, follow up, and seek another route if needed
options.consequence: You keep the path to support open.

options.text: Give up and assume nothing is available
options.consequence: Polite persistence and alternate routes keep support reachable; giving up assumes a 'no' that may not be final.

scenarios.debrief: Persist politely and seek other routes when a service is slow; don't give up on the support your child needs.

scenarios.hook: Match each right or support to where it applies.
scenarios.relearn: Reasonable accommodation, a support plan and family understanding each apply where your child needs championing.

scenarios.hook: A relative whispers that your child's diagnosis is 'a punishment' or 'karma'. You want to shut it down kindly.
scenarios.relearn: Naming that it's no one's fault and no punishment protects both you and your child from cruel, baseless blame.

yourLine.text: "It's no one's fault and no punishment, it's just how his brain works, and he's wonderful."
"Maybe, I do wonder what we did wrong."

scenarios.hook: Sort: a true, shame-lifting statement, or a harmful blame myth?
scenarios.relearn: 'You didn't cause this' and 'your child can thrive' lift shame; blaming mothers and 'hide it' are harmful.

scenarios.hook: Spot the move that frees a family from shame.
scenarios.relearn: Free your family from shame by accepting it's no one's fault and focusing on support, not endless self-blame.

scene.text: Accepting it's no one's fault
Blaming yourself endlessly
Focusing energy on support

scenarios.why: Accepting it's no one's fault and focusing on support free a family; endless self-blame keeps them stuck.

scenarios.hook: You feel pressure to keep your child's diagnosis a secret from everyone.
scenarios.relearn: Choose openness on your terms over total secrecy; hiding it carries the shame it's trying to avoid.

options.text: Share it on your own terms with people who can support you
options.consequence: You let understanding and help in.

options.text: Keep it hidden and carry it alone
options.consequence: Sharing on your terms lets in understanding and help; total secrecy isolates you and quietly reinforces the stigma.

scenarios.debrief: Share the diagnosis on your own terms with supportive people; total secrecy isolates you and feeds stigma.

scenarios.hook: Your child is fixated on one topic and others call it 'obsessive'. You want to honour it.
scenarios.relearn: Honouring an intense interest as a strength to feed builds confidence, unlike dismissing it as 'obsessive'.

yourLine.text: "That deep interest is a strength, let's feed it, it might become something amazing for you."
"Enough of that, talk about normal things."

scenarios.hook: After a meltdown has passed, your child seems ashamed. You want to reconnect with warmth.
scenarios.relearn: Reconnecting after a meltdown with reassurance, not reproach, rebuilds safety and self-worth.

yourLine.text: "That was a hard moment and it's over, you're not in trouble, I'm here and I love you."
"See what happens when you don't control yourself?"

scenarios.hook: Sort: builds a neurodiverse child's confidence, or erodes it?
scenarios.relearn: Naming strengths and celebrating wins build confidence; problem-only focus and comparisons erode it.

scenarios.hook: Match each sign to what your child may need.
scenarios.relearn: Overwhelm, anxiety and a lit-up interest each tell you what your child needs: calm, preparation, or encouragement.

scenarios.hook: Spot what nurtures a neurodiverse child's self-worth.
scenarios.relearn: Nurture a neurodiverse child's self-worth by seeing their gifts and loving who they are, not listing deficits.

scene.text: Seeing and naming their gifts
Treating them as a list of deficits
Loving them for exactly who they are

scenarios.why: Seeing their gifts and loving who they are nurture self-worth; treating them as deficits erodes it.

scenarios.hook: You're exhausted and a friend asks how you really are. You want to be honest, not brush it off.
scenarios.relearn: Being honest that it's hard and you need support opens the door to the help that sustains you for your child.

yourLine.text: "Honestly, it's hard and I'm tired, I love him fiercely and I could use some support too."
"Oh, we're totally fine, no problems at all."

scenarios.hook: Sort: sustains a parent for the long haul, or burns them out?
scenarios.relearn: Sharing the load and a support network sustain you; doing it all alone and never asking burn you out.

scenarios.hook: Match a parent need to the support for it.
scenarios.relearn: Loneliness, needing strategies and running on empty each have a support: peers, professionals, and your own wellbeing care.

scenarios.hook: Your child's grandparent wants to help but doesn't understand the diagnosis. You want to guide them in.
scenarios.relearn: Warmly explaining and giving a concrete way to help turns a willing grandparent into real support, not a closed door.

yourLine.text: "Here's a simple way to understand him, and here's exactly how you can help, he adores you."
"Just don't get involved if you don't understand it."
